posts.text:
THIS IS HUGE. Democrats started asking who got paid to build Trump’s ballroom. Last night he signed an order telling every federal contractor in the country to clear it with the White House before answering Congress.

Start with what set it off. Senator Richard Blumenthal, who will chair a key Senate investigative panel in January, has been writing to the companies working on the White House ballroom. He asked the construction firm what the thing is going to cost and how it got picked for the job. Ordinary questions. Public money.
Then Friday night, this.

The executive order tells contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House of any congressional request for information, to coordinate their answers with the administration, and to withhold anything the White House decides is privileged.

And if they do not go along, the order says their contracts can be terminated and their future work with the government suspended.

Read that again. Not a legal argument. A threat to the company’s revenue.

The White House fact sheet says certain congressional leaders are “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government.”

Asking a contractor what a job costs is not harassment. It is the entire point of oversight.

This is not happening on its own either. On Monday the White House counsel told federal agencies they need his approval before anybody testifies before Congress. He wrote to Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on House Oversight, and suggested some of these investigations may amount to “blatant criminality.” He also reminded Democrats they are not in the majority yet, so they cannot make anyone comply.

That is true for about six more weeks.

Here is what all of this tells you. A White House that had nothing to hide would let the ballroom contractor answer a question about the ballroom.

In January, Blumenthal gets subpoena power. So does Garcia. The questions do not go away because Trump signed a piece of paper on a Friday night.

🇺🇸 Stephen Miller is reportedly closing the White House side door that let advisers keep their private paychecks while working in government

The door has a name, "special government employee." 

It lets someone from the private sector join an administration for up to 130 days a year without giving up outside income, and most never have to disclose their clients.

The new chief of staff has told associates he wants it used sparingly and prefers full-time hires, people familiar with the plan told the Wall Street Journal. 

Clinton and Biden aides used the same status, so this isn't a one-party habit.

The timing explains it.

Polls showed self-dealing claims hurt Republicans in the midterms, and Democrats take over the oversight committees in January with letters already going out. 

Tightening up now is smart housekeeping.

It won't stop the hearings about who was paid by whom, but "we already fixed that" is a far better answer under oath than anything else on offer.

Well played by Miller.

Source: WSJ / Writer: Daniel

Young software developers are losing ground in the AI era.

US software developer employment among workers aged 22 to 25 has fallen about 20% since November 2022, when ChatGPT launched, per Stanford Digital Economy Lab.

22–25: −20%
26–30: −4%
31–34: +6%
35–40: +11%
41–49: +20%

That’s a 40-percentage-point gap between the youngest and the most experienced developers.
